items.title: 68089_John Malachi oral history interview
items.q: Harold showed me a lot about how Teddy Wilson was playing, because he played that style himself.

ctx.x: In the interim of this, there were some pianists around town that I liked very much. There was one guy, a fellow from New York who had come down here and he made Washington his home for a number of years. His name was Harold Francis. Later he worked with the Ink Spots for a while. I think he died in the Fifties. Anyway, Harold was probably the most literate of the Black pianists around town, because at that particular time there were a lot of good piano players around, but none of them could read very well.

Harold used to play a lot of shows at the Howard Theatre, and at times he would substitute for Earl Hines or some of the other pianists at the Howard Theatre that came to the dances. Because it was kind of proper for the leaders, if they were pianists, to play a few numbers and have a substitute pianist. They would go off the bandstand -- where they would go, I don't know. Then they would come out and maybe play another specialty. Harold showed me a lot about how Teddy Wilson was playing, because he played that…
There was also another fellow around that I used to listen to a lot, although he played more like Earl Hines. He's still around, a fellow named Dick Hopkins. I listened to him a lot.
